title: Surinder Kumar Wadhwa vs Amrish Gupta on 6 January, 2026
full_text: Surinder Kumar Wadhwa vs Amrish Gupta on 6 January, 2026 IN THE COURT OF Ms. AASTHA SHARMA, LD. JMIC (N.I. Act)-03, SOUTH-EAST DISTRICT, SAKET COURTS COMPLEX: DELHI Surinder Kumar Vs. Amrish Gupta CC No. 6446/2017 U/S 138 Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 1. CNR number DLSE020089312017 2. Name of the complainant Sh. Surinder Kumar Wadhwa, S/o Late Sh. D.C. Wadhwa, R/o C-191, Defence Colony, New Delhi-110024. 3. Name of the accused person(s), parentage Sh. Amrish Gupta, & residential address CC No. 6446/2017 Surinder Kumar Vs. Amrish Gupta Page 1 of 20 Digitally signed by AASTHA SHARMA AASTHA Date: SHARMA 2026.01.06 19:11:26 +0530 S/o Sh. R.K. Gupta, R/o D-3, Geetanjali Enclave, New Delhi -110017 Also at: Khasra No. 638, Bandh Road, Village Gadaipur, New Delhi - 110030 4. Offence complained of or proved U/s 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 5. Plea of the accused Pleaded not guilty and claimed trial 6. Final Judgment/order Convicted 7. Date of judgment/order 06.01.2026. Date of Institution : 30.05.2017 Date of Reserving Judgment/Order : 19.12.2025 Date of Pronouncement of Judgment/Order : 06.01.2026 CC No. 6446/2017 Surinder Kumar Vs. Amrish Gupta Page 2 of 20 Digitally signed by AASTHA SHARMA AASTHA Date: SHARMA 2026.01.06 19:11:32 +0530 ARGUING COUNSELS: Ld. Counsel for the complainant : Sh. Kanhaiya Singhal Ld. Counsel for the Accused : Sh. Arjun Sanjay and JUDGMENT 1. Vide this judgment, this Court shall dispose of the present complaint filed by the complainant Sh. Surinder Kumar Wadhwa (hereinafter referred to as "the Complainant") against Sh. Amrish Gupta (hereinafter referred to as "the Accused") under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 read with Section 142 of Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (hereinafter referred to as " NI Act "). Brief facts of the case: 2. It is the case of the complainant, A. That, the complainant and the accused had good personal relations and the accused used to obtain personal loans from the complainant on several occasions and the complainant used to keep an account of the same. That on 23.12.2016, the accused reconciled his loan with the complainant and issued a confirmation certificate in respect of interest amount and outstanding loan amount of Rs. 6,52,95,000/- recoverable from him, which was signed and issued by the accused. That, when the complainant requested the accused to pay the principal amount with the interest, the accused ensured final payment of Rs. 6,75,60,000/- to the complainant and accordingly issued two post dated cheques bearing no. 350445 CC No. 6446/2017 Surinder Kumar Vs. Amrish Gupta Page 3 of 20 Digitally signed by AASTHA SHARMA AASTHA Date: SHARMA 2026.01.06 19:11:37 +0530 dated 07.04.2017 for Rs. 5 crore drawn on Axis Bank Ltd., Nehru Place, New Delhi and cheque no. 612410 dated 07.04.2017 for Rs. 1,75,60,000/- drawn on Citi Bank, Delhi and assured the complainant that the cheques would be honoured on their representation to the bank. B. That, upon assurance by the accused, the complainant presented the aforementioned cheques in his bank account ICICI Bank, S-266, Defence Colony, New Delhi-110024. However, to the shock of the complainant, the same were returned as dishonoured with the remarks "Payment Stopped by Drawer" vide return memo dated 10.04.2017. C. In these circumstances, the complainant got issued a statutory legal demand notice to the accused through his counsel, dated 01.05.2017, thereby requiring the accused to pay the amount of the aforesaid cheque within a period of 15 days from the receipt of the said notice. The said notice under Sec. 138 of NI Act was sent to the accused through Registered AD/Speed Post/Courier at his correct address. That despite service of the above stated notice of demand, the Accused has deliberately and wilfully failed to comply with the said notice of demand and has failed to pay the amount of the aforesaid cheque within the stipulated period of 15 days from the date of receipt of the said notice. Consequently, this case was filed by the complainant against the accused persons, which was within the limitation period as laid down u/s 138 , NI Act. CC No. 6446/2017 Surinder Kumar Vs. Amrish Gupta Page 4 of 20 Digitally signed by AASTHA SHARMA AASTHA Date: SHARMA 2026.01.06 19:11:42 +0530 3. In the pre-summoning evidence, the Authorised representative of the complainant examined himself as CW-1 on affidavit being Ex. CW1/A and placed on record documents Ex. CW1/1 to Ex. CW1/10. 4. Upon prima facie consideration of the pre-summoning evidence, the accused person was summoned. 5. Upon the appearance of the accused, notice under Section 251 CrPC was served upon him on 06.12.2018 to which he pleaded not guilty. At this stage, the accused admitted that he issued the cheques in question and also admitted his signatures therein. He has admitted to receiving the legal demand notice. He stated that he had taken a loan from the complainant and the blank signed cheques in question were handed over to the complainant as security against the outstanding liability of the accused in 2015. The accused has further stated that he had also handed over title deeds of his property to the complainant as security and later on, he had cleared his entire liability towards the complainant by paying the amount in the account of son and wife of the complainant. The accused has further stated that he infact had to take money from the complainant and when he asked the complainant to return his cheques in question, the complainant said that he had lost these cheques, which is when he gave instructions to his banker to stop payment against these cheques. The accused has further stated that an FIR has been registered against the complainant by the accused with EOW. The accused has further stated that the complainant has misused these cheques in question and filed a false case against him. CC No. 6446/2017 Surinder Kumar Vs. Amrish Gupta Page 5 of 20 Digitally signed by AASTHA SHARMA AASTHA Date: SHARMA 2026.01.06 19:11:47 +0530 6. Thereafter CW-1 was examined, cross-examined and discharged. Vide order of the court, CE was closed. Accordingly, matter proceeded to the stage of recording the statement of the accused. 7. Statement of accused under Section 313 CrPC read with Section 281 CrPC was recorded on 21.11.2022 wherein the accused stated that he wishes to lead DE. Thereafter DW-1, DW-2, DW-3 and DW-4 were examined, cross-examined and discharged and vide order of this court, DE was closed on 05.06.2024. 8. Vide order of Hon'ble HC of Delhi dated 06.11.2024, application u/s 311 CrPC to summon and examine COW-1 Ms. Neena Wadhwa and COW-2 Sh. Siddhartha Wadhwa was allowed. COW-1 and COW-2 were cross-examined by both the parties and discharged on 12.12.2024. 9. Thereafter, the matter proceeded to the stage of final arguments. Final arguments heard and written submissions considered on behalf of both the parties. Record perused and considered. 10. It is well settled position of law that to constitute an offence under Section 138 , NI Act, the following ingredients are required to be fulfilled: I. drawing of the cheque by a person on an account maintained by him with a banker, II. The cheque was issued for payment to another person for discharge in whole/part any debt or liability; CC No. 6446/2017 Surinder Kumar Vs. Amrish Gupta Page 6 of 20 Digitally signed by AASTHA AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2026.01.06 19:11:52 +0530 III. Cheque has been presented to the bank within a period of six months from the date on which it is drawn or within the period of its validity whichever is earlier. RBI in its notification DBOD.AML BC.No.47/14.01.001/2011-12 has reduced the aforesaid period from 6 months to 3 months. IV. Returning of the cheque unpaid by the drawee bank for want of sufficient funds to the credit of the drawer or any arrangement with the banker to pay the sum covered by the cheque; V. Giving notice in writing to the drawer of the cheque within 30 days of the receipt of information by the payee from the bank regarding the return of the cheque as unpaid demanding payment of the cheque amount; VI. Failure of the drawer to make payment to the payee or the holder in due course of the cheque, of the amount covered by the cheque within 15 days of the receipt of the notice. The offence under Section 138 , NI Act is made out against the drawer of the cheque, only when all the aforementioned ingredients are fulfilled. 11. Analysing all the concerned provisions of law and various pronouncements in this regard, the Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of Basalingappa v. Mudibasappa [AIR 2019 SC 1983] held that: I. Once the execution of cheque is admitted, Section 139 of the Act mandates that a presumption be drawn that the cheque in question was for the discharge of any debt or other liability. CC No. 6446/2017 Surinder Kumar Vs. Amrish Gupta Page 7 of 20 Digitally signed by AASTHA SHARMA AASTHA Date: SHARMA 2026.01.06 19:11:57 +0530 II. The presumption under Section 139 is a rebuttable presumption and the onus is on the accused to raise the probable defence. The standard of proof for rebutting the presumption is that of preponderance of probabilities. III. To rebut the presumption, it is open for the accused to rely on evidence led by him or accused can also rely on the materials submitted by the complainant in order to raise a probable defence. Inference of preponderance of probabilities can be drawn not only from the materials brought on record by reference to the circumstances upon which they rely. IV. That it is not necessary for the accused to come in the witness box in support of his defence. Section 139 imposes an evidentiary burden and not a persuasive burden. It is therefore implied that the law regarding the presumption for the offence under Section 138 , NI Act, the presumptions under Section 118(a) and Section 139 have to be compulsorily raised as soon as the execution of cheque by the accused is admitted or proved by the complainant and thereafter the burden is shifted upon the accused to prove otherwise. Appreciation of evidence and marshalling of facts: 12. Issuance of cheque: The complainant has filed on record the original cheque, i.e., bearing no. 350445 dated 07.04.2017 for Rs. 5,00,00,000/- drawn on Axis Bank Ltd., Nehru Place, New Delhi and cheque bearing no. 612410 dated 07.04.2017 for Rs. 1,75,60,000/- drawn on Citi Bank, New Delhi (Ex. CW1/3 and CC No. 6446/2017 Surinder Kumar Vs. Amrish Gupta Page 8 of 20 Digitally signed by AASTHA SHARMA AASTHA Date: SHARMA 2026.01.06 19:12:03 +0530 Ex. CW1/4 respectively). In notice under Section 251 CrPC, the accused has admitted that the cheques in dispute belong to him. It is also not disputed that the cheques in question are not drawn on the account maintained by the accused person and it is impliedly admitted therefore that the accused is the drawer of the cheques. Therefore, ingredient number I stands fulfilled in the present case. 13. Presentment and dishonor of cheque: As per the RBI guidelines, it is essential for the cheque in question be to presented within a period of three months from the date on which they are drawn and the same be returned as unpaid by the drawee bank for want of sufficient funds to the credit of the drawer or any arrangement with the banker to pay the sum covered by the cheque. In the case at hand, the cheques in question were returned vide return memo dated 10.04.2017 (Ex. CW1/5 & Ex. CW1/6 respectively) due to the reason "Payment Stopped by Drawer." By implication thereof, the cheques were presented within three months and the same were returned. Therefore, Ingredient number III & IV stand fulfilled in the present case. 14. Legal demand notice and payment by the accused thereof: The legal notice dated 01.05.2017 (Ex. CW1/8) was dispatched on 02.05.2017 vide Speed Post (Ex. CW1/9), i.e., within 30 days of return of the bank memo indicating cheques in question being unpaid. The fact that the legal demand notice has made a clear and unambiguous demand for payment of the cheque in question is not disputed. The accused has admitted to the receipt of legal demand notice in notice u/s 251 CrPC. Further, as per the presumption raised under Section 114 of Indian Evidence Act, 1872 and Section 27 of General Clauses Act, if the legal demand notice is sent at CC No. 6446/2017 Surinder Kumar Vs. Amrish Gupta Page 9 of 20 Digitally signed by AASTHA AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2026.01.06 19:12:07 +0530 the correct address, then the same shall be deemed to have been duly served, as per the precedent laid down by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in C.C. Alavi Haji v. Palapetty Muhammed , (2007) 3 SCC (Cri). The ingredient number V is fulfilled by virtue of giving of legal demand notice within 30 days from the bank return memo. The receipt of legal demand notice by the accused is deemed to be admitted as per the discussion above. 15. Moving on, it is not disputed that the accused has not made the payment of the cheque amount within 15 days of the receipt of legal demand notice. Therefore, ingredient number VI also stands fulfilled in the present case. Presumption under Section 118A read with Section 139 , NI Act 16. The NI Act raises two presumptions in favour of the holder of the cheque, i.e., complainant; firstly, with regard to the issuance of cheque for consideration, as contained in Section 118(a) and secondly, with regard to the fact that the holder of cheque received the same for discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability, as contained in Section 139 of the Act. These presumptions shall end only when the contrary is proved by the accused, that is, the cheque was not issued for consideration and in discharge of any debt or liability etc. The Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in its judgment titled Rangappa Vs. Sri Mohan , (2010) 11 SCC 441 held that a reverse onus clause usually imposes an evidentiary burden and not a persuasive burden and when an accused has to rebut the presumption under Section 139 , the standard of proof for doing so is that of "preponderance of probabilities". Therefore, if the accused is able to raise a CC No. 6446/2017 Surinder Kumar Vs. Amrish Gupta Page 10 of 20 Digitally signed by AASTHA SHARMA AASTHA Date: SHARMA 2026.01.06 19:12:13 +0530 probable defence which creates doubts about the existence of a legally enforceable debt or liability, the prosecution can fail. It was further held that the accused can rely on the materials submitted by the complainant in order to raise such a defence and it is conceivable that in some cases the accused may not need to adduce evidence of his/her own. Once a probable defence is raised, then the onus is shifted to the complainant to establish that a legally enforceable liability existed in his favour and the burden of proof on the complainant in this case is that of "beyond reasonable doubt." 17. The accused can rebut the presumption as raised under Section 138 , NI Act by: (a) putting forth his defence at the time of framing of notice u/s 251 CrPC; (b) cross-examining the complainant; (c) when statement of accused is recorded u/s 313 CrPC; (d) or by leading defence evidence, thereby demolishing the case of the complainant. Rebuttal of Presumption by Accused as to existence of legally enforceable debt 18. In light of the above discussion, since the accused has admitted to issuance of cheques, admitted the signatures on the cheques and legal notice has also been deemed to be served, what is left to be seen is whether the accused has been able to rebut the presumption against him, i.e., whether the accused is able to raise a CC No. 6446/2017 Surinder Kumar Vs. Amrish Gupta Page 11 of 20 Digitally signed by AASTHA AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2026.01.06 19:12:20 +0530 probable defence which creates doubts about the existence of a legally enforceable debt? 19. In the present case, in order to discharge his initial burden to prove the abovementioned ingredients, the complainant relied upon the affidavit of the complainant being Ex. CW1/A and placed on record documents mentioned hereinbefore. While, the defence of the accused is based on the following legs; which shall be discussed individually below: 19.1 Security cheques issued by the accused in the year 2013 and 2015 were misused by the complainant. It is the case of the accused that the cheques in question were issued by the accused in the year 2013 and 2015 for transactions related to M/s Blue Ice Farm between the parties and other financial transactions pending between the parties, which have no relation to the transaction in question. The accused has also mentioned the same in his FIR No. 27/2018 (Mark DW1/A). The accused has further argued that cheque bearing no. 350445 drawn on Axis Bank was part of the cheque book which was issued to the accused in the year 2013-14 and the accused would not issue one single leaf out of that cheque book in the year 2016-2017 for another transaction when he is already using another chequebook. The accused has also relied upon the testimony of DW-4 bank witness for the same. The accused has made the same argument for cheque bearing no. 612410 drawn on Citi Bank, to indicate that the cheques in question were issued in 2013 and 2015, and not 2017. CC No. 6446/2017 Surinder Kumar Vs. Amrish Gupta Page 12 of 20 Digitally signed by AASTHA AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2026.01.06 19:12:25 +0530 It has been held in Sunil Todi v. State of Gujarat (2021) 12 SC CK 0012 that a post-dated cheque issued for security, if dishonoured also amounts to an offence u/s 138 , NI Act, if on the date of dishonour of the cheque, there exists some legally enforceable liability. It is to be noted that the accused in his notice u/s 251 CrPC and at the stage of DE, has admitted that he had issued the cheques in question as security for the loan of Rs. 9 crore taken from the complainant. Therefore, the argument of the accused that security cheque issued for some other transaction cannot be used for present loan transaction does not stand, if there existed any legally enforceable liabilities qua the present loan against the accused. Furthermore, the accused has repeatedly taken the defence that it was orally decided between the parties that the security cheques issued for the loan taken by the accused shall be returned by the complainant when the original title deeds of the property M/s Blue Ice Farms Pvt. Ltd. will be handed over to the complainant. The accused as DW-1 has stated that he had handed over the title deeds to the complainant in the year 2013, while the accused at the stage of notice u/s 251 CrPC has stated that he had handed over the security cheques in question in the year 2013 and 2015 for the loan taken from the complainant. It is to be noted that if the agreement was for the complainant to return the security cheques once the title deeds are handed over to the complainant by the accused, and if the title deeds were handed over to the complainant in the year 2013, then why would the accused issue security cheques qua the present loan in the year 2015. The same is contradictory to the defence taken by the accused. CC No. 6446/2017 Surinder Kumar Vs. Amrish Gupta Page 13 of 20 Digitally signed by AASTHA AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2026.01.06 19:12:31 +0530 Therefore, this argument of the accused that the cheques in question were issued for some other purpose other than the present liability does not hold ground. 19.2 Certificate dated 23.12.2018, i.e., Ex. CW1/2 is false and fabricated document The accused has argued that the certificate Ex. CW1/2 has been issued on 23.12.2018, i.e., before the financial year while the other certificates issued by the accused and also admitted by the accused are after 31st March and therefore Ex. CW1/2 is a false and fabricated document. Further, the accused has argued that the amount mentioned in the ledger Ex. CW1/1 does not match with Ex. CW1/2 as the accused had repaid Rs. 2,10,00,000/- till 23.02.2016, however the certificate indicates that only a sum of Rs. 67,95,000/- has been paid. At the outset, it is to be noted that the case of the complainant is that both the parties had reconciled their accounts qua their liabilities after which it was determined that the accused owes the liability as mentioned in the certificate Ex. CW1/2. It is relevant to note that it is nowhere mandated in law to reconcile the accounts or issue a certificate qua liability only at the end of the financial year. The certificate in question is a transaction between the lender and the borrower and the same has been issued for reconciliation of accounts by the accused. The accused cannot escape his liability only by stating that the same is forged and fabricated as the same has not been issued at the end of the financial year unlike other certificates on record. Further, the accused has merely disputed his signatures on Ex. CW1/2 by making a bald statement, however neither the original certificate was called by the CC No. 6446/2017 Surinder Kumar Vs. Amrish Gupta Page 14 of 20 Digitally signed by AASTHA SHARMA AASTHA Date: SHARMA 2026.01.06 19:12:37 +0530 accused nor any handwriting expert was summoned and examined to assess the credibility of the signatures on Ex. CW1/2. Moreover, prima facie, the signatures appear to be consistent with the admitted signatures of the accused on other judicial documents. Therefore, this argument of the accused holds no ground as well in absence of any documentary proof to invalidate the certificate dated 23.12.2018. 19.3 Accused does not owe any outstanding liability to the complainant in light of debt being repaid to the wife and son of the complainant at the instance of the complainant It is the case of the accused that after the payment of Rs. 2,10,00,000/- to the complainant in the year 2016, he had repaid the remaining sum to the wife and son of the complainant, i.e., Neena Wadhwa and Siddharth Wadhwa respectively, at the instance of the complainant and therefore he does not owe any liability towards the complainant. It is to be noted that the accused as DW-1 has admitted his liability and has stated as follows: "...I took money about Rs. 9 crores from him starting 2013 and gave some security cheques against the money taken as loan. I have returned more than the cheques amount to the complainant which includes Rs. 8,64,00,000/- to wife and son of the complainant by way CC No. 6446/2017 Surinder Kumar Vs. Amrish Gupta Page 15 of 20 Digitally signed by AASTHA SHARMA AASTHA Date: SHARMA 2026.01.06 19:12:42 +0530 of cheques. I can produce the bank statement as I have not brought the same today..." The accused has further stated: "..I do not remember the date, month and year as to when Rs. 8,64,00,000/- to wife and son of the complainant was given. Vol. The bank statement already reflect the same which I have not brought today. I had also given some other amount to the complainant also.." The accused however has only made bald statements qua the repayment of the sum to the wife and son of the complainant and has nowhere placed on record any proof for the same. The accused has also not placed on record bank account statement or cheque number qua which the payment was made to the wife and son of the complainant. In light of the same, the accused has merely made bald statements without raising a probable defence of repayment of the liability on direction of the complainant. It is to be noted that the onus of proof would have shifted on the complainant to prove that the amount paid by the accused to wife and son of complainant is for property by placing agreement to sell on record, only if the accused had raised a probable defence, which the accused has failed to do. Therefore, the argument of the accused that the wife and son of the complainant did not place on record agreement to sell does not hold ground in absence of the accused showing any proof to indicate repayment of his admitted liability. CC No. 6446/2017 Surinder Kumar Vs. Amrish Gupta Page 16 of 20 Digitally signed by AASTHA AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2026.01.06 19:12:47 +0530 Furthermore, the argument of the accused that the wife and son of the complainant have made several contradictions in their testimony as COW-1 and COW-2 in the present case and in the recovery proceedings before Hon'ble High Court of Delhi regarding financial assistance from the accused does not go to the root of the matter and the same does not make the witnesses incredible. It is a well settled law that if any changes are to be made in an agreement, the same amounts to novation u/s 62 of Indian Contract Act, 1872 and the same is done only with the mutual consent of all parties involved and leads to earlier contract being substituted completely. In the absence of proof regarding novation, it cannot be assumed that there was any novation of contract between the parties. Therefore, the defence of the accused that the repayment was made to the wife and son of the complainant at the instance of the complainant becomes devoid of any merit, since the complainant has refused that there was any such agreement. Consequently the accused person has failed to prove the novation and in the absence of novation the loan amount was to be returned to the complainant only and no other person. Be that as it may, as discussed above the accused person has even failed to prove that he made any payment to the wife and son of the complainant. 19.4 Amount mentioned on the cheque in question does not amount to the legally enforceable liability and therefore the complaint is not maintainable Ld. Counsel for the accused submits that the accused has made substantial payment of Rs. 2,10,00,000/- between 01.06.2016 to 01.10.2016 and despite the CC No. 6446/2017 Surinder Kumar Vs. Amrish Gupta Page 17 of 20 Digitally signed by AASTHA AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2026.01.06 19:12:53 +0530 same, the complainant has calculated interest at the principal sum of Rs. 7,55,00,000/- at 12% p.a. and the interest should have been charged at the reduced principal amount after deducting Rs. 2,10,00,000/-, which would make the due liability of the accused lesser than the amount mentioned on the cheque in question and therefore the present complaint is not maintainable in terms of Dasrathbhai Trikambhai Patel v. Hitendra Mahendrabhai Patel, SC 2022. Per contra, Ld. Counsel for the complainant submits that it was orally decided between the complainant and the accused that the accused shall pay interest at Rs. 6,65,00,000/- at 16% p.a. and the same did not fluctuate with the change in principal amount and the accused has paid 16% interest on the amount of Rs. 6,65,00,000/- from the period of 14.10.2013 to 01.12.2015. Subsequent to that, the accused availed further financial assistance of Rs. 90,00,000/- on which interest was charged and then it was orally decided between the parties that after 01.01.2026, the accused shall pay interest at 12% p.a. on the amount of Rs. 7,55,00,000/- and the accused continued to pay the interest on the same principal amount. It is argued by the Ld. Counsel for the complainant that the accused usually faltered on paying interest monthly and if the same would have been added in the principal sum of the accused, then the amount of interest would go higher which is why the interest was calculated on a fixed sum. It is to be noted at the outset that the accused in his ITR for the financial year 2016-17 has mentioned his outstanding liability of unsecured loan as Rs. 7,55,00,000/- which is the exact sum on the ledger as placed on record by the complainant (Ex. CW1/1 (Colly.)). It indicates that the accused had impliedly CC No. 6446/2017 Surinder Kumar Vs. Amrish Gupta Page 18 of 20 Digitally signed by AASTHA SHARMA AASTHA Date: SHARMA 2026.01.06 19:13:00 +0530 admitted his liability. Furthermore, the accused at the stage of notice u/s 251 CrPC and DE has admitted that he had taken a loan from the complainant, however there is no proof of repayment of the same apart from bald allegations made by him. The accused in his testimony as DW-1 has been evasive in his responses and has responded stating "I will check and revert" for several documents which have been placed on record by him, such as certificate dated 02.05.2016 Ex. CW1/DX. Moreover, the accused has responded evasively even when questioned about the date and mode of repayment of the outstanding liability to the wife and son of the complainant. In absence of any other substantial defence available to the accused, the accused cannot escape his liability merely by questioning the ledger or the calculation of the complainant qua interest charged in the ledger. It is to be noted that the term of interest was decided orally between the parties and the same is substantiated by documentary evidence placed on record by the complainant and nothing contrary has been placed on record by the accused qua the same. Furthermore, perusal of ledger maintained by the accused Ex. CW1/DY also indicates the liability of the accused as Rs. 7,45,00,000/- till 01.10.2016 which is similar to the liability as claimed by the complainant in his ledger. The principle of Dasrathbhai (supra) is that "for the commission of offence u/s 138 , NI Act, the cheque that is dishonoured must represent a legally enforceable debt on the date of maturity or presentation." As per the ledger Ex. CW1/1, the amount mentioned as closing balance on 31.03.2017 was Rs. 6,75,60,000/-. Therefore, the amount mentioned on the cheque in question on the date of its presentation was the amount mentioned as closing balance on the date of the presentation of the cheque in CC No. 6446/2017 Surinder Kumar Vs. Amrish Gupta Page 19 of 20 Digitally signed by AASTHA AASTHA SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2026.01.06 19:13:05 +0530 question. In light of the documentary evidence placed on record by the complainant, the argument of the accused that the cheque in question is more than the legally enforceable liability of the accused holds no ground as well. 20. In the present case, the accused has failed to even create any doubt, let alone discharging his burden of proof to rebut the presumption u/s 138 , NI Act. The accused has neither brought any witness nor any documentary evidence on record to substantiate his claim. It is the duty of the accused to punch holes in the story of the complainant which he has not been able to do. On the other hand, the complainant has brought documentary evidence to prove his version of the story along with the benefit of presumption u/s 139 , NI Act in his favour. 21. In light of the discussion above, ingredient no. II has been fulfilled in the present case. 22. Accordingly, Accused Amrish Gupta is held guilty and is convicted of the offence under Section 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act. 23. Copy of this judgment be given to the convict free of cost as per rules.
